item.title: Behold this decorated image — A heap of wounds, a collection of sores, Diseased, the object of many lustful thoughts, Nothing stable or permanent here.…
item.description:
Behold this decorated image —
A heap of wounds, a collection of sores,
Diseased, the object of many lustful thoughts,
Nothing stable or permanent here.

Behold this adorned appearance,
With jewels and earrings,
A skeleton covered by skin,
Made beautiful by clothes.

The feet are painted with lac and dye,
The face is smeared with powder and paste —
Enough to fool a fool,
But not one who seeks the far shore.

The hair is curled in seven rings,
The eyes are rubbed with collyrium and rouge —
Enough to fool a fool,
But not one who seeks the far shore.

Like a newly decorated medicine box,
This foul body is adorned for the occasion —
Enough to fool a fool,
But not one who seeks the far shore.

The hunter set his trap and snare,
The wise deer does not approach,
Having eaten the crops, we go our way,
Leaving the trapper to lament.

From: Majjhima Nikāya 82 – Raṭṭhapālasutta

item.title: “Monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being. And what, monks, is not yours? The eye, monks,…
item.description:
“Monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being. And what, monks, is not yours? The eye, monks, is not yours — abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being. Forms are not yours — abandon them. Eye-consciousness is not yours — abandon it. Eye-contact is not yours — abandon it. Suppose, monks, a person were to carry away, burn, or do whatever they want with all the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in this Jeta’s Grove. Would you think: ‘This person carries us away, burns us, or does whatever they want with us’?” - “No, venerable sir.” - “Why not?” - “Because that is not our self nor belonging to our self.” - “So too, monks, the eye is not yours — abandon it … Forms … Eye-consciousness … Eye-contact … Whatever feeling arises dependent on mind-contact — pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant — that feeling is not yours. Abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.101

item.title: “And what, monks, is the origin of suffering? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact…
item.description:
“And what, monks, is the origin of suffering? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling. With feeling as condition, craving. This is the origin of suffering. Dependent on the ear … on the nose … on the tongue … on the body … Dependent on the mind and phenomena, mind-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling. With feeling as condition, craving. This, monks, is the origin of suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.106

item.title: “And how, monks, is there restraint? Here, monks, when a monk sees a form with the eye, he is not attached to agreeable forms nor…
item.description:
“And how, monks, is there restraint? Here, monks, when a monk sees a form with the eye, he is not attached to agreeable forms nor repelled by disagreeable forms. He dwells with bodily mindfulness established, with an immeasurable mind. He knows as it actually is the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. Here, evil, unwholesome states that have arisen are abandoned without remainder. When he tastes a flavor … When he cognizes a phenomenon with the mind, he is not attached to agreeable phenomena nor repelled by disagreeable phenomena. He dwells with bodily mindfulness established, with an immeasurable mind. He knows as it actually is the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. Here, evil, unwholesome states that have arisen are abandoned without remainder. Thus, monks, is restraint.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.244

item.title: “Good sirs, what is suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, sickness is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, despair are suffering, not…
item.description:
“Good sirs, what is suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, sickness is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, despair are suffering, not getting what one wants is suffering; in short, the five clinging-aggregates are suffering. This, good sirs, is called suffering. Good sirs, what is the origin of suffering? It is craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence. This, good sirs, is called the origin of suffering.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 9 – Sammādiṭṭhisutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Fear, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. Suffering, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. Disease, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. A…
item.description:
“Fear, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. Suffering, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. Disease, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. A boil, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. Clinging, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. A bog, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. And why, monks, is fear a synonym for sensual pleasures? Monks, infatuated by sensual desire, bound by sensual desire, one is not free from fear in this very life, nor free from fear in the future. Therefore, fear is a synonym for sensual pleasures.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.23

item.title: Māra: You will not escape, You will not escape this world. What use is this practice of seclusion to you? Enjoy sensual pleasures — Do…
item.description:
Māra:

You will not escape,
You will not escape this world.
What use is this practice of seclusion to you?
Enjoy sensual pleasures —
Do not have regrets later.

Elder Nun Selā:

Sensual pleasures are like swords and spears —
They cut the aggregates to pieces.
What you call the pleasure of life —
For me, that sensual pleasure
Is no longer enticing.

Everywhere, delight is destroyed.
The mass of darkness,
The blinding darkness, has been shattered.
Know this, O Evil One —
You are Māra,
You are defeated.

From: Therīgāthā 3.7

item.title: Elder Tissa: “As if struck by a sword, As if his head were on fire, Mindful, a monk should go forth, Abandoning sensual lust.”
item.description:
Elder Tissa:
“As if struck by a sword,
As if his head were on fire,
Mindful, a monk should go forth,
Abandoning sensual lust.”

From: Theragāthā 1.39

item.title: “Monks, just as a defiled, dusty cloth, if placed in clean water becomes clean, if placed in a furnace becomes clean. So too, monks, a…
item.description:
“Monks, just as a defiled, dusty cloth, if placed in clean water becomes clean, if placed in a furnace becomes clean. So too, monks, a monk of such virtue, such quality, such wisdom – even if he eats almsfood of choice rice with black grains removed, various soups and curries – that does not become an obstacle for him.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 7 – Vatthūpamasutta

item.title: “Venerable sirs, for one who has abandoned lust for form, abandoned desire, abandoned love, abandoned thirst, abandoned passion, abandoned craving — when that form changes…
item.description:
“Venerable sirs, for one who has abandoned lust for form, abandoned desire, abandoned love, abandoned thirst, abandoned passion, abandoned craving — when that form changes and alters, no sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, or despair arise. For feeling … perception … formations … For one who has abandoned lust for consciousness, abandoned desire, abandoned love, abandoned thirst, abandoned passion, abandoned craving — when that consciousness changes and alters, no sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, or despair arise. Seeing this benefit, venerable sirs, our Teacher speaks of the subduing of desire and lust for form … for feeling … for perception … for formations; our Teacher speaks of the subduing of desire and lust for consciousness. And because one attains and dwells in wholesome states, living at ease in this very life, without obstruction, without distress, without fever, and at the breakup of the body, after death, one will be reborn in a good destination. Therefore, this is the accomplishment of wholesome states praised by the Blessed One.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.2
